sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Cone-rod dystrophies (CRD) represent a group of inherited pigmentary retinopathies where cone photoreceptor degeneration precedes rod involvement. Unlike Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP), which starts with night blindness (rod-first), CRD patients typically present early with decreased visual acuity, photophobia, and dyschromatopsia. Prevalence is estimated at 1:30,000 to 1:40,000. Progression is generally more rapid and severe than in isolated cone dystrophies.

rows: Most common form; ABCA4 mutations also cause Stargardt disease.
GUCY2D is a common cause of early-onset severe CRD.
Often associated with high myopia and rapid progression.
Associated with syndromic presentations like MELAS.

sections.title: Primary Clinical Symptoms
content: Early central vision loss (decreased BCVA)
Severe Dyschromatopsia (Protan/Deutan or Tritan defects)
Intense Photophobia (Hemeralopia)
Central Scotoma on visual field testing
Late-onset Nyctalopia (night blindness)
Peripheral constriction (later stages)

branches: Temporal pallor of the Optic Disc

rows: Sensitive marker for early cone dysfunction.
Indicates secondary rod involvement (distinguishes from pure CD).

sections.title: Multimodal Imaging Findings
content: FAF: Perifoveal hyper-autofluorescent ring (early) or foveal hypo-autofluorescence (atrophy).
OCT: Loss of Ellipsoid Zone (EZ) and Interdigitation Zone; thinning of the ONL.
OCT: 'Foveal cavitations' may be seen in early stages.
Visual Fields: Central/paracentral scotoma which eventually breaks through to periphery.

sections.title: Management & Low Vision Protocol
content: Step 1: Genetic Testing & Counseling (Confirm molecular diagnosis/inheritance).
Step 2: Photoprotection (Strict UV-blocking sunglasses & wide-brimmed hats to reduce phototoxicity).
Step 3: Low Vision Rehabilitation (Magnifiers, electronic reading aids, telescopic lenses).
Step 4: Avoid High Dose Vitamin A (In ABCA4-related cases, can be toxic/pro-lipofuscin).
Step 5: Regular Screening for Complications (Cystoid Macular Edema, Cataracts).
Step 6: Referral to Clinical Trials (Gene therapy, optogenetics, cell-based therapies).

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Sudden vision drop: Rule out CNV or Macular Hole.
High dose Vitamin A supplementation in ABCA4 patients (May accelerate lipofuscin accumulation).
Rapidly progressive vision loss in children (Rule out Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis).
Unexplained Photophobia: Always perform ERG if fundus looks normal.

sections.title: Memory Aid: The 3 C's of CRD

content.explanation: C - Color vision defects early; C - Central scotoma early; C - Cones worse than Rods (Photopic ERG < Scotopic ERG).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A 'Normal fundus' does not rule out CRD; early cases require ERG for diagnosis.
The 'Bull's Eye' is not pathognomonic; consider toxicity and Stargardt.
ABCA4 mutations are pleomorphic; they can cause Stargardt, CRD, or RP phenotypes.
Unlike RP, CRD patients often struggle more in bright light than in dim light early on.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
sections.content: Recent research focuses on Gene Therapy (targeting GUCY2D and ABCA4) and Pharmacological interventions like Emixustat or ALK-001 to reduce lipofuscin levels. The 'ProgStar' study provided critical natural history data for ABCA4-related diseases, which is now being used to design primary endpoints for clinical trials. Optogenetics remains a promising field for end-stage CRD to restore light sensitivity to remaining retinal cells (bipolar/ganglion cells).
